examples: Without the internet, modern society could not function.
Without his help, this project probably won't succeed.
Without evidence, we cannot find him guilty.
Without practice, improvement is impossible.
Without funding, the research cannot continue.
Admission is not possible without a reservation.
fields.explain:
Used when you want to affirm that N is “indispensable” to an action/result.
Suitable for presentations, reports, and descriptions of systems and procedures (expresses a condition-consequence relationship).
The second clause is usually a verb of ability/possibility of existence: できない・ありえない・成り立たない・難しい.
Not used to express a deliberate act of “doing something without N” (in that case use “N なしで V”).
The subject can be general/subjective; however, the nuance leans toward an objective judgment.

• The pattern “～なしでは～ない” expresses a necessary condition: without N, the following action/result cannot happen, is very unlikely to happen, or does not exist.
• Objective nuance, a general evaluation of how necessary N is (a foundation, condition, means, or resource).
• The second clause is usually a negation of ability/possibility: できない・ありえない・成り立たない・進まない・語れない・理解できない.
• Formality: usable in both written and spoken language; often used in written language, scientific explanations, and journalism to state a necessity.
• Unlike “N なしで”, which simply means “without having/using N”, “N なしでは” implies “because N is missing, it is impossible”.
fields.notes:
• N is usually a fundamental element: 資金・計画・説明・理解・協力・技術・データ・証拠・準備・許可.
• In policy/regulation sentences, this pattern makes the statement more decisive and is common in notices: 許可なしでは入れません.
• Emphatic variants: ～なしではやっていけない (cannot get by), ～なしでは語れない (cannot be discussed or mentioned without).
mistakes: Confusing it with “N なしで”: “なしで” only means “without N” and does not imply “cannot”. The JLPT often sets traps with these two patterns.
Using an affirmative second clause: you need ない／できない／難しい… If the second clause is affirmative, the nuance is wrong.
Choosing an unsuitable noun: with something that is not a necessary condition, “なしでは” sounds forced.
Confusing it with “なしには”: the meanings are close, but “なしには” is slightly more formal/stiff and often goes with abstract action nouns (努力・説明).

rows: <ruby>証拠<rt>しょうこ</rt></ruby>なしでは<ruby>判断<rt>はんだん</rt></ruby>できない
Stiffer nuance; often goes with abstract action nouns (<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>・<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>)
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>なしには<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>しない
Written language; emphasizes that without N it cannot happen
<ruby>信頼<rt>しんらい</rt></ruby>なくしてはチームは<ruby>成<rt>な</rt></ruby>り<ruby>立<rt>たた</rt></ruby>たない
<ruby>朝食<rt>ちょうしょく</rt></ruby>なしで<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけた
If not A, then not B
General condition pattern, not limited to nouns
<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>てみないことには<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>からない

examples: Without effort, dreams do not come true.
You may not enter the room without permission.
Without a thorough explanation, customers won't be satisfied.
Without agreement, the plan cannot move forward.
Without data, the discussion cannot even begin.
Without preparing in advance, you can't keep up with the class.
fields.explain:
Choose an N that is a required condition/procedure, something “procedural” or “fundamental” (許可・同意・説明・検証・準備).
Normative, decisive nuance; suitable for notices, procedures, and business work.
Can be used as “～ことなしには” to make written language more formal.
Not used if you only want to say “did it without N” (use “N なしで”).

• “～なしには～ない” = “unless there is N / without N, cannot/does not happen”.
• Stronger and more formal nuance than “～なしでは”; often used when N is a necessary action/procedure (努力・説明・合意・準備・許可).
• The second clause is a negative form of ability/progress: できない・ありえない・進まない・始まらない・成立しない.
• Often appears in regulations, theses, and business guidelines to emphasize a mandatory condition.
fields.notes:
• The form “Vることなしには” emphasizes the procedural nature: 確認することなしには出荷しない.
• In advertising/PR, it may be used to emphasize a standard: 身分証なしには購入できません.
• To sound softer in conversation, you can replace it with “N がないと～ない”.
mistakes: Mixing it up with “なしで”: the JLPT often sets the pair 許可なしで/許可なしには as a trap. Choose “なしには” when the second clause means “cannot/may not”.
Using an affirmative second clause: a negative is required (ない・できない・進まない…).
Choosing an unsuitable N (not a condition/procedure) makes the sentence sound forced. Example: “花なしには勉強できない” is usually unnatural.
Confusing the nuance with “なしでは”: both are correct in meaning, but when an exam asks about a formal/normative nuance, “なしには” is preferred.

rows: Formal/stiff; often used with action/procedure nouns
<ruby>合意<rt>ごうい</rt></ruby>なしには<ruby>進<rt>すす</rt></ruby>めない
More neutral; widely used for conditions/resources
<ruby>資金<rt>しきん</rt></ruby>なしでは<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>められない
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>なくしては<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>なし
<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>なしで<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めた
If not A, then not B
Extends to clauses, not limited to nouns
<ruby>試<rt>ため</rt></ruby>してみないことには<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>からない

fields.connection: N + ならいざ知らず / V/A plain form + (の)なら
examples: It might be different for a child, but it is shameful for an adult to do such a thing.
If it were a joke, that would be one thing, but I cannot seriously accept such a demand.
That may have worked in the old days, but that approach no longer works today.
An expert might be able to, but an amateur probably cannot judge it.
It might work with a small group, but this method is impossible on the scale of 100 people.
On a vacation it would be different, but on a business trip there is no time for sightseeing.
fields.explain:
Used to present an “acceptable hypothetical exception” and then reject the actual situation.
Stays polite but has a nuance of criticism; avoid using it directly with superiors/customers if possible.
Often combined with evaluation words: 恥ずかしい・受け入れられない・無理だ・通用しない・難しい・すべきではない.
The first clause is usually a noun: 冗談・子ども・昔・専門家・少人数・試作品など.

• “～ならいざ知らず” = “if it were ~, it would be somewhat acceptable/understandable, but … (is unsuitable/hard to accept/impossible)”.
• Expresses a hypothetical contrast: sets up an understandable case in order to emphasize that the current reality is unacceptable.
• Nuance of criticism/polite argument, somewhat archaic/written language; used when you want to keep distance and stay objective.
• The second clause is usually a negative judgment, a prohibition, a criticism, or “does not apply/is not accepted”.
fields.notes:
• “いざ知らず” originally means “I cannot say about ~” and developed into a hypothetical concession that emphasizes the negation in the second clause.
• Often found in essays/expert opinions to avoid direct criticism while still keeping a position.
• A similar inversion can be made by using “～ならともかく”: its nuance is lighter than “ならいざ知らず”.
mistakes: Using it with an affirmative/positive second clause: wrong nuance. The second clause should be negative/hard to accept.
Using it with the subject “I/we” to talk about yourself sounds unnatural, because the nuance criticizes other people/general matters.
Confusing it with “ならまだしも”: exams set traps with these two patterns; “ならいざ知らず” is more formal and carries the meaning “I cannot say about ~”.
Placing it after a long, complex verb: prefer a short, concise noun in the first clause so the sentence sounds more natural.

rows: If it were ~, it would be less bad, but…
Formal, somewhat written; presents a hypothetical exception
<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>ならいざ<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らず、<ruby>社会<rt>しゃかい</rt></ruby><ruby>人<rt>じん</rt></ruby>は…
If it were ~, it would be acceptable, but…
<ruby>遅刻<rt>ちこく</rt></ruby>はまだしも、<ruby>無断<rt>むだん</rt></ruby><ruby>欠勤<rt>けっきん</rt></ruby>はだめだ
The second clause is not necessarily negative
<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>た<ruby>目<rt>め</rt></ruby>はともかく、<ruby>味<rt>あじ</rt></ruby>はいい
Comparison against expectations, no hypothetical exception
<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもにしては<ruby>上手<rt>じょうず</rt></ruby>だ

examples: Children think about things in their own way, as children.
If you're going, then prepare properly for it.
Even if it's cheap, it has its uses as a cheap item.
If I can't do it, I'll still do my best within my limits.
He is busy, so he finds ways of coping that suit his busy schedule.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes appropriateness, without comparing beyond one's level; avoids excessive complaining.
Can be used in polite criticism: ～なら～なりにしなさい/考えなさい.
“～なりの N” is used to make it concrete: 自分なりの答え, 会社なりの方針.
The tone can be admonishing, sometimes a little stern.

• Appropriateness/propriety: “If …, then (do/can) … in the way/at the level of …”.
• Adapting to conditions: adjusting expectations/actions to suit the circumstances and level.
• Implied limitation: acknowledges limits but still has its own value/way (according to ability, budget, age, level...).
• Advisory usage: used to give gentle advice or indirect criticism.
fields.notes:
• Repeating the same element before and after “なら/なりに” is the characteristic feature of the structure.
• Often combined with a contrast to expectations: 安いなら安いなりに（それ相応の）品質だ.
• In formal writing, “～なりの + N” appears more often, to nominalize the criterion of appropriateness.
mistakes: Dropping the repetition: “子どもなら自分なりに” is incorrect when the matching “子どもなら子どもなりに” is needed.
Using it for extreme praise or criticism: the pattern accepts limitations; it does not make absolute statements.
Confusing it with ～に応じて: the JLPT often asks you to distinguish the nuance of “appropriate/befitting”.
Wrong form “Adj-ななら Adj-ななりに” (the correct form keeps “な” only once: 静かなら静かなりに).

rows: Neutral, objective; does not imply “if you're going to …, do … properly”.
<ruby>予算<rt>よさん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>応<rt>おう</rt></ruby>じて<ruby>選<rt>えら</rt></ruby>ぶ。
Focuses on quantity/limitation; lacks the nuance of “appropriateness”.
できるだけ<ruby>頑張<rt>がんば</rt></ruby>る。
A common branch of this pattern; emphasizes the agent doing it “by oneself”.
<ruby>自分<rt>じぶん</rt></ruby>なりに<ruby>工夫<rt>くふう</rt></ruby>する。
Carries an evaluation; does not form a repeated pair like ～なら～なりに.

examples: Would you like something to drink, like coffee or tea?
If you're stuck, either ask the teacher or look it up in the library.
On days off, let's refresh ourselves by watching a movie or taking a walk.
If you're free, you could play a game or read a book.
Please send the documents by email or fax.
If anything comes up, please call or send a message.
fields.explain:
The two listed items should be of the same type (both nouns or both verbs in the dictionary form).
Emphasizes “a concrete action” rather than just listing information.
The nuance can be a bit pushy; use it with equals/acquaintances. With customers/superiors, choose a softer way.
Usually accompanied by an ending that expresses a suggestion/mild command.

• Presents two (or more) choices, “for example A or B”, implying “any way is fine, choose one and do it”.
• Nuance of a mild to moderate suggestion/request; sometimes it feels like urging “do something”.
• Used in instructions, advice, or polite suggestions; not neutral like とか/や, and stronger in terms of “action”.
• The sentence often ends with してください／したらどうですか／しなさい／しよう／すればいい.
fields.notes:
• In polite language, the ending can be changed to ～してはいかがでしょうか／～されてはどうでしょうか to reduce the pressure.
• “A なり B なりして” is a very natural frame for advising the listener to “do something”.
• When listing more than two, three items can be used, but keep the rhythm concise and avoid wordiness.
mistakes: Mixing word classes: “N なり Vる なり” is unnatural; they must be of the same type (N-N, V-V).
Using it to describe a one-time past event with no sense of suggestion → とか/や is a better choice.
Confusing it with “Vるなり” meaning “as soon as…”; exams often set traps with this pair.
Using the bare command form as is with superiors/customers sounds rude; switch to a polite form of suggestion.

rows: For example A or B, doing either is fine
Suggests an action, mild nuance of urging
<ruby>医者<rt>いしゃ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くなり<ruby>薬<rt>くすり</rt></ruby>を<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>むなりしなさい
Neutral, does not push for action
<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>とか<ruby>雑誌<rt>ざっし</rt></ruby>とかを<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>む
A different grammar point, not a listing
<ruby>席<rt>せき</rt></ruby>に<ruby>座<rt>すわ</rt></ruby>るなり<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>てしまった

examples: In an emergency, do not be misled by false rumors.
In a recession, securing cash flow is the top priority.
In the late Edo period, commerce developed.
In his position, the utmost care is required in what he says.
Even in a harsh situation, they did not stop trying.
fields.explain:
Placed at the beginning of a sentence to set the context for an argument/recommendation.
Combines with nouns such as: 非常時／緊急時／不況下／戦時／現場／立場／制度下.
Avoid it in casual speech because it sounds too formal.

• Indicates an era, circumstance, or position; used to state what should be done/what is characteristic within that framework.
• Serious nuance, suitable for regulations, reports, and research papers.
• The form ～にあっても adds a contrasting clause to emphasize will/persistence.
fields.notes:
• In legal/administrative language, ～にあっては often goes with a command/condition: ～しなければならない／～こと.
• “不況下にあっては” is a model phrase in economic commentary.
• The past form is rarely used; it is mainly used in the present to describe general norms.
mistakes: Applying it to a noun that is not a context: × 公園にあっては → use 公園では.
Confusing the particles: にあっては ≠ においては; exams often test choosing the right nuance.
Using it in ordinary conversation makes the sentence heavy and unnatural.

rows: Spoken language; does not emphasize norms.
<ruby>緊急<rt>きんきゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>時<rt>とき</rt></ruby>では<ruby>冷静<rt>れいせい</rt></ruby>に。
Formal but neutral; puts little emphasis on a “special condition”.
<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>において<ruby>報告<rt>ほうこく</rt></ruby>する。
A theoretical/regulatory viewpoint; differs from the actual context.
<ruby>制度<rt>せいど</rt></ruby><ruby>上<rt>うえ</rt></ruby><ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>はない。

examples: That is a remark unbecoming of a teacher.
A mistake unworthy of a doctor occurred.
They were severely punished for misconduct unbecoming of a civil servant.
That is an attitude unbecoming of a parent.
His abusive language is unbecoming of a leader.
fields.explain:
Extremely formal and critical; avoid it in casual communication unless emphasizing morality.
Often combined with nouns for “behavior”: 行為・発言・態度・振る舞い・不祥事・ミス.
Usually placed right before the noun being evaluated: N1にあるまじきN2.
The classical feel (あるまじき) creates a strong normative impression and sometimes sounds “harsh”.

• Expresses behavior/an attitude that is “unacceptable, unworthy” of a position, profession, or moral standard.
• Strong criticism, often seen in the news, codes of ethics, and official statements.
• N1 is a role: 教師・医者・公務員・親・学生・政治家・社会人… N2 is 発言・行為・態度・ミス・不祥事, etc.
fields.notes:
• From the archaic “あるまじき” = あるべからざる; belongs to the same semantic field of moral taboos.
• Favored in newspaper headlines to emphasize the degree of seriousness.
• Can be used for self-criticism, but easily gives a dramatic impression: 私も教師にあるまじき言動をしてしまった。
mistakes: Wrong word order: × あるまじき教師の発言 → ○ 教師にあるまじき発言.
Using it with a target that is not a “role/status”: × 天気にあるまじき → not appropriate.
Confusing the degree with ～にふさわしくない: あるまじき is stronger and carries moral condemnation.
Leaving out the noun after あるまじき makes the sentence incomplete: an N2 such as 行為・発言 is needed to complete it.

rows: Milder and more neutral than あるまじき.
<ruby>教師<rt>きょうし</rt></ruby>にふさわしくない<ruby>態度<rt>たいど</rt></ruby>。
Expresses a personal opinion, less normative.
<ruby>医者<rt>いしゃ</rt></ruby>とは<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>えない<ruby>振<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>る<ruby>舞<rt>ま</rt></ruby>い。
General admonition; あるまじき is stronger and morally critical.
そんな<ruby>発言<rt>はつげん</rt></ruby>をすべきではない。
Emphasizes the emotion of “shame”; strong in degree, but not as classical as あるまじき.
<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>として<ruby>恥<rt>は</rt></ruby>ずべき<ruby>行為<rt>こうい</rt></ruby>。

fields.meaning: Only when… for the first time…
examples: Only after becoming a teacher did I understand how complex students' feelings are.
Only as the person in charge on site do you truly feel the weight of decisions.
Only at 30 did I see the path I should take.
Only after starting work did the importance of time management really sink in.
Only when you become a parent yourself do you understand how much you owe your parents.
fields.explain:
Formal, with a depth of experience; suitable for reflective or inspirational writing.
Avoid using it with a trivial/meaningless milestone; it should be a “turning point”.
Often goes with idioms of strong feeling: 身に染みる・痛感する・骨身にこたえる.

Meaning: “Only when (reaching) N does … happen for the first time”. Emphasizes an important/noteworthy milestone, suggesting that it came late, was hard to reach, or that experience/strict conditions were needed to obtain the result/realization.
• N: a point in time (40歳, 入社三年目), a status (親, 社会人, プロ), a setting (現場, 海外).
• Second clause: achieving/realizing something for the first time (～ようになる／分かる／悟る／実感する／達成する).
• Used a lot in written language, essays, memoirs, and interviews about experiences.
fields.notes:
• Repetitive structure that adds weight: ～にして初めて、～と分かった／～ことに気づいた.
• Can be combined with ordinal numbers to emphasize lateness: 三度目にして初めて合格した。
• In headlines/interviews: “現場にして初めて見えた真実”.
mistakes: Using it with an N that is not a “milestone” → the meaning becomes vague.
Confusing it with Vて初めて when the milestone is a concrete action → Vて初めて is more natural.
Using it for a random, one-time event with no “accumulation” → not suitable.

rows: Only after doing V, for the first time…
Common, conversational; emphasizes the action V
<ruby>働<rt>はたら</rt></ruby>いて<ruby>初<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めて<ruby>税金<rt>ぜいきん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>重<rt>おも</rt></ruby>さを<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>った。
<ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>になって<ruby>初<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めて<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かった。
It is precisely by V that there is value
Usually states a general truth/value, not only “the first time”
<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>してこそ<ruby>成長<rt>せいちょう</rt></ruby>できる。
A negative condition, not a “first-time turning point”
<ruby>登録<rt>とうろく</rt></ruby>してからでないと<ruby>利用<rt>りよう</rt></ruby>できない。
